turns.content: Determine gcd(P(n), P(n+1)) for an arbitrary integer n.
Next analyze gcd(P(n), P(n+2)). Use a linear combination that eliminates the quadratic term, then determine how the gcd depends on n modulo 7.
Carry out the analogous analysis for gcd(P(n), P(n+3)), including the relevant reduction modulo 3.
For positive integers a and b, call {P(a), P(a+1), ..., P(a+b)} fragrant. Translate this definition into an equivalent condition involving pairwise common factors.
Represent the terms of a block as vertices, joining two vertices exactly when the corresponding values have gcd greater than 1. Which graph property is equivalent to the block being fragrant?
Using the graph criterion you just established together with the gcd results, decide whether a fragrant block can contain exactly four consecutive values P(a), P(a+1), P(a+2), and P(a+3).
Apply the same graph criterion to five consecutive values P(a), P(a+1), ..., P(a+4). Decide whether they can form a fragrant block and make clear where the congruence conditions become incompatible.
Construct an explicit fragrant block of six consecutive values. You may use the Chinese remainder theorem; give the starting value a and identify a common-factor partner for every term.
Check the congruences used in your six-term construction and verify directly that each of its terms shares a nontrivial factor with another term in the block.
Complete the lower-bound argument by explaining why blocks with fewer than four terms are also impossible, and summarize what the four- and five-term analyses establish.
Combine the lower bound with the explicit construction. What is the smallest possible size of a fragrant set?
